lungs-smog.title: Protecting your lungs on smog days
lungs-smog.summary: Cut your exposure to fine particles when air quality is poor.

content.text: Before you go outside
Check your local Air Quality Index before heading out, and limit prolonged or heavy outdoor exertion when it is high.
Keep windows and doors closed during peak smog hours to reduce indoor particle levels.
If you must be outside
A well-fitted N95/FFP2 mask reduces the fine particles you inhale during heavy smog.
Indoors, a HEPA air purifier can lower fine-particle concentrations.
Avoid adding indoor smoke — cigarettes, incense, or unventilated cooking — on top of outdoor smog.

lungs-indoor-air.title: Indoor air quality on polluted days
lungs-indoor-air.summary: Keep the air inside cleaner while outdoor smog is high.

content.text: Reduce indoor sources
Most indoor air pollution comes from combustion — cooking smoke, candles, incense and tobacco — so cutting these sources matters as much as sealing out the smog outside.
Use an extractor fan or open a window briefly while cooking, then reseal the room once smoke has cleared.
When outdoor air improves
Ventilate during the cleanest part of the day (check your AQI trend) rather than leaving windows open continuously.
Never use an unvented gas or charcoal appliance indoors — it can raise indoor pollution and carbon-monoxide risk sharply.

asthma-poor-air.title: Managing asthma when air quality is poor
asthma-poor-air.summary: Stay ahead of flare-ups on high-pollution days.

content.text: Stay ahead of a flare-up
Keep your reliever (rescue) inhaler with you and follow your written asthma action plan.
Move exercise indoors or to cleaner-air times of day when the Air Quality Index is high.
At home
Reduce indoor triggers: no smoking indoors, manage dust, and keep indoor air as clean as possible.
If symptoms worsen — frequent coughing, wheezing or breathlessness — seek medical care promptly.

asthma-poor-air.sourceName: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

asthma-action-plan.title: Building your asthma action plan
asthma-action-plan.summary: A written plan turns a bad day into a manageable one.

content.text: What a plan covers
A written asthma action plan sets out your daily medicines, the early warning signs of a flare-up, and exactly what to do at each stage — agreed in advance with your clinician.
Keep a copy where you can find it quickly, and share one with a family member or housemate.
Reviewing it
Revisit the plan with your clinician after any flare-up, or at least once a year, so it stays matched to how your asthma is behaving.
A plan is guidance, not a diagnosis — always follow your own clinician's instructions over general guidance like this.

asthma-action-plan.sourceName: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

when-to-stay-indoors.title: When to stay indoors (Air Quality Index)
when-to-stay-indoors.summary: What each AQI band means for outdoor activity.

content.text: Reading the bands
AQI 0–50 (Good): air quality is satisfactory; no precautions needed.
AQI 51–100 (Moderate): unusually sensitive people should consider limiting prolonged outdoor exertion.
AQI 101–150 (Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups): sensitive groups (children, older adults, heart/lung conditions) should reduce prolonged outdoor exertion.
When it gets serious
AQI 151–200 (Unhealthy): everyone should reduce prolonged outdoor exertion; sensitive groups should avoid it.
AQI 201+ (Very Unhealthy/Hazardous): avoid outdoor activity and stay indoors with clean air where possible.

aqi-pm-sizes.title: Understanding PM2.5 vs PM10
aqi-pm-sizes.summary: The two particle sizes behind most AQI readings, explained.

content.text: What the numbers mean
PM2.5 (particles under 2.5 micrometres) travel deepest into the lungs and bloodstream and drive most health guidance; PM10 (under 10 micrometres) affects the upper airway more.
On a smoggy day, PM2.5 is usually the number worth checking — it is the more sensitive signal.
Where they come from
Vehicle exhaust, industrial smoke and burning are common PM2.5 sources; dust and pollen contribute more to PM10.

extreme-heat.title: Staying safe in extreme heat
extreme-heat.summary: Reduce heat-illness risk during hot spells.

content.text: Through the day
Drink water regularly through the day, even before you feel thirsty.
Avoid the sun during the hottest hours and limit strenuous activity.
Keep your living space cool — shade windows, ventilate at night.
Warning signs
Watch for heat exhaustion (dizziness, headache, nausea); move to a cool place, rest and rehydrate, and seek help if it does not improve. Never leave children or pets in a parked vehicle.

heat-exhaustion-vs-stroke.title: Recognizing heat exhaustion vs heat stroke
heat-exhaustion-vs-stroke.summary: Know the difference — one of them is a medical emergency.

content.text: Heat exhaustion
Heavy sweating, dizziness, headache, nausea and cool clammy skin. Move to shade or air conditioning, loosen clothing, and rehydrate with water.
Heat stroke
Hot, dry or flushed skin, confusion, or loss of consciousness are signs the body has stopped regulating its temperature.
Heat stroke is a medical emergency. Call for emergency help immediately and cool the person while waiting — do not wait to see if it improves.

who-asthma.title: Asthma
who-asthma.summary: WHO's fact sheet on asthma — what it is, how common it is, and how it is managed.

content.text: WHO's asthma fact sheet describes what asthma is, how widespread it is, the symptoms it causes, and the broad principles behind long-term treatment and avoiding triggers.
It is written for a general audience rather than for clinicians, and it does not replace a treatment plan agreed with your own doctor.
ForeSeeMe links to this fact sheet rather than reproducing it, so what you read is the current text as WHO publishes it.

who-copd.title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
who-copd.summary: WHO's fact sheet on COPD, including air pollution and smoke among its risk factors.

content.text: WHO's COPD fact sheet covers what the condition is, the breathing symptoms associated with it, and the risk factors it identifies — which include tobacco smoke and both outdoor and household air pollution.
It is background reading on the condition, not a diagnosis or a treatment plan.
ForeSeeMe links to this fact sheet rather than reproducing it, so what you read is the current text as WHO publishes it.

who-cardiovascular.title: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs)
who-cardiovascular.summary: WHO's fact sheet on heart and circulatory disease and the risk factors behind it.

content.text: WHO's cardiovascular diseases fact sheet covers what conditions the term includes, how much illness they account for worldwide, and the behavioural and environmental risk factors associated with them.
It is general public-health information; anything about your own heart health belongs with your clinician.
ForeSeeMe links to this fact sheet rather than reproducing it, so what you read is the current text as WHO publishes it.

who-ambient-air-pollution.title: Ambient (outdoor) air pollution
who-ambient-air-pollution.summary: WHO's fact sheet on outdoor air pollution and the health effects linked to it.

content.text: WHO's ambient air pollution fact sheet sets out where outdoor pollution comes from, which pollutants are measured, and the respiratory and cardiovascular health effects associated with exposure to them.
It is the authority behind the air-quality guidance elsewhere in this catalogue, and the place to read the full picture.
ForeSeeMe links to this fact sheet rather than reproducing it, so what you read is the current text as WHO publishes it.

who-household-air-pollution.title: Household air pollution
who-household-air-pollution.summary: WHO's fact sheet on indoor air pollution from cooking and heating fuels.

content.text: WHO's household air pollution fact sheet covers pollution produced inside the home — largely by cooking and heating with solid fuels and kerosene — and the health effects associated with it.
It complements the outdoor air-quality guidance: on a bad-air day, indoor sources add to what comes in from outside.

who-heat-and-health.title: Heat and health
who-heat-and-health.summary: WHO's fact sheet on how heat affects health and who is most at risk.

content.text: WHO's heat and health fact sheet covers how high temperatures affect the body, which groups are most at risk during hot weather, and the measures public-health authorities recommend for protection.
